title: Six Gates on logic Ports with always_comb
description:
### Problem statement
This exercise builds the six basic gates over the same three inputs, using the SystemVerilog style the rest of this track follows: every port is declared `logic` and the outputs are driven from one `always_comb` block. Hand-check all eight truth-table rows before writing any code, because each gate disagrees with its neighbours in a different row.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_gate_bank_logic(
    input  logic a,
    input  logic b,
    input  logic c,
    output logic w_and,
    output logic w_or,
    output logic w_nand,
    output logic w_nor,
    output logic w_xor,
    output logic w_xnor
);
```

#### Requirements
- Drive all six outputs from one `always_comb` block; do not use `assign` statements.
- `w_and` and `w_or` are the plain three-input AND and OR.
- `w_nand` and `w_nor` are high exactly when the matching plain gate is low.
- `w_xor` is high for an odd count of high inputs; `w_xnor` is high for an even count.

#### Notes
In Verilog this module mixes `wire` outputs with `assign` statements. In SystemVerilog `logic` covers both roles, and `always_comb` replaces `always @(*)`: the tool infers the sensitivity list for you, so a forgotten input can no longer leave the block stale.
starter_code:
module sv_gate_bank_logic(
    input  logic a,
    input  logic b,
    input  logic c,
    output logic w_and,
    output logic w_or,
    output logic w_nand,
    output logic w_nor,
    output logic w_xor,
    output logic w_xnor
);
    // TODO: drive all six outputs from one always_comb block

endmodule
solution_hints: Write the eight input rows on paper and mark what each of the six gates says in every row.
Each output needs exactly one procedural assignment inside the always_comb block; six assignments total.
XOR answers whether the count of high inputs is odd; NAND and NOR are the inverted AND and OR.

title: Two-to-One Mux in an always_comb Block
description:
### Problem statement
Select between two single-bit sources with `sel`: 0 routes `a` to `y`, 1 routes `b` to `y`. The point of the exercise is the procedural style: the selection lives in an `always_comb` block and the output is declared `logic`, with no continuous assignment anywhere in the module.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_mux2_comb(
    input  logic a,
    input  logic b,
    input  logic sel,
    output logic y
);
```

#### Requirements
- `sel = 0` drives `y` from `a`; `sel = 1` drives `y` from `b`.
- The assignment must sit inside an `always_comb` block; no `assign` and no gate primitives.
- A conditional operator or an if-else are both acceptable.

#### Notes
The Verilog version of this mux declares the output `reg` and uses `always @(*)`, and the reg keyword misleads beginners into thinking a register is involved. `always_comb` with an `output logic` port says exactly what is meant: combinational logic on a 4-state variable, no sensitivity list to maintain.
solution_hints: The mux never inspects a or b; only sel decides which source reaches y.
The conditional operator reads condition, value-when-true, then value-when-false.
Decide once whether sel 1 belongs to the true arm or the false arm, then keep that convention.

title: Implement the Timing: Toggle Flip-Flop Tour
description:
### Problem statement
A toggle flip-flop halves a clock: while `t` is high, `q` inverts on every rising edge; while `t` is low, `q` holds. The grader applies each table row as one clock cycle, in order, and samples after that cycle's edge; register state carries over between rows. Trace the table by hand first, then write the `always_ff` block that produces it.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_toggle_ff(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic t,
    output logic q
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n` is an asynchronous active-low reset that clears `q` immediately.
- On each positive clock edge with `rst_n` high: `t = 1` inverts `q`, `t = 0` leaves `q` unchanged.
- Use one `always_ff` block with a nonblocking assignment.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | t | q after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

#### Notes
Plain Verilog writes `always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)` and cannot tell the tool whether the block was meant to be sequential. `always_ff` declares the intent, so a synthesis tool rejects the same block if it contains no edge; Icarus accepts the keyword and treats it exactly like the equivalent always block.
solution_hints: Reset is checked first inside the block; only the else branch toggles or holds.
Toggling is q <= ~q, but only under the t condition; otherwise nothing is assigned and q holds.
Keep the sensitivity list at posedge clk or negedge rst_n so the reset stays asynchronous.

title: Fix: Parity Typed with the Wrong Reduction
description:
### Problem statement
`odd` must be 1 whenever `data` holds an odd number of ones. The current code compiles and runs, but it answers a different question entirely: it reports whether every bit of the byte is set. Find the wrong reduction operator and repair the single line inside the `always_comb` block.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_reduction_op(
    input  logic [7:0] data,
    output logic       odd
);
```

#### Requirements
- `odd` is 1 when `data` contains 1, 3, 5 or 7 ones, and 0 otherwise.
- Fix the operator inside the existing `always_comb` block; do not restructure the module.
- The fix is one character; no extra logic is needed.

#### Timing table (first rows)

| data | ones | odd |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 | 0 |
| 7 | 3 | 1 |

#### Notes
The reduction operators fold a whole vector to one bit: AND-reduction asks whether all bits are set, OR-reduction asks whether any bit is set, and XOR-reduction asks whether an odd number are set. The broken code picked the wrong one from the family, which is exactly the kind of typo that compiles silently in both Verilog and SystemVerilog.
solution_hints: Check the second row by hand: data is 00000001, so the answer must be 1, but the current code says 0.
Three reduction operators exist, one per gate; only one of them answers the odd-count question.
Parity over a vector is the XOR-reduction: a single prefix operator on the whole bus.

title: Two-State Enum Machine: IDLE and RUN
description:
### Problem statement
Build the smallest useful state machine: an `S_IDLE` state that waits for `go`, and an `S_RUN` state that is held until reset. The states are `typedef enum logic [1:0]` literals declared inside the module, the transitions live in `always_ff`, and the `busy` output is a comparison against the state in `always_comb`. The grader applies each row as one clock cycle and samples after the edge; state carries over.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fsm_idle_run(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic go,
    output logic busy
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef enum logic [1:0] {S_IDLE, S_RUN} state_t;` inside the module and one `state_t state;` register.
- `rst_n` asynchronously returns the machine to `S_IDLE`.
- `go = 1` moves `S_IDLE` to `S_RUN` on the clock edge; `S_RUN` holds until the next reset.
- `busy` is 1 exactly while the machine is in `S_RUN`, assigned in `always_comb`.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | go | busy after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 6 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 10 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

#### Notes
The Verilog habit is `localparam IDLE = 2'b00;` with a `reg [1:0] state`. The enum version gives the same encodings plus real type checking: assigning a stray integer to `state` or comparing against a typo'd constant becomes a tool-visible error instead of a silent bug, and waveforms can show state names instead of raw bits.
solution_hints: The transition block needs only the reset branch and one if on go; the RUN state holds by doing nothing.
busy never appears in the sequential block; it is a comparison evaluated against the current state.
In always_comb write busy = (state == S_RUN); the parentheses document that a state is being tested.

title: Checker: Parity Verdict as an Enum Result
description:
### Problem statement
A checker that only says pass or fail wastes information. This one recomputes parity over the 7-bit word `d` and compares it with the delivered bit `p`: a match is verdict `P_OK`, a mismatch with odd data parity is `P_ODD`, and a mismatch with even data parity is `P_EVEN`. The three verdicts are `typedef enum logic [1:0]` literals declared in the module, and the output carries the same encoding.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_parity_enum(
    input  logic [6:0] d,
    input  logic       p,
    output logic [1:0] verdict
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef enum logic [1:0] {P_OK, P_ODD, P_EVEN} verdict_t;` inside the module.
- Recompute the parity of `d` with a reduction XOR; `P_OK` when it equals `p`.
- On a mismatch, `P_ODD` when the data parity is odd, `P_EVEN` when it is even.
- The numeric output values are the literal encodings: 0, 1 and 2.

#### Notes
Verilog checkers return bare numeric codes and rely on comments to explain what 2 means. Defining the codes as enum literals costs one typedef line and gives every reader, waveform and lint tool the same named vocabulary for the result.
solution_hints: First compute a single bit: the XOR-reduction of d says whether the word holds an odd number of ones.
The verdict question is then a two-way branch: does that bit agree with p, and if not, which side is it on.
P_OK is the match case; the two mismatch names split on the value of the recomputed parity bit.

title: Four-to-One Mux with case and default
description:
### Problem statement
Route one of four single-bit sources to the output: `sel = 0` picks `a`, 1 picks `b`, 2 picks `c` and 3 picks `d`. The selection is a `case` on `sel` inside `always_comb`, and the `default` arm is written explicitly even though the two select bits make it unreachable, because the habit keeps wider case statements safe.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_mux4_case(
    input  logic       a,
    input  logic       b,
    input  logic       c,
    input  logic       d,
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    output logic       y
);
```

#### Requirements
- One `case (sel)` inside an `always_comb` block, with an arm per select code.
- Include `default: y = 1'b0;` even though sel cannot leave the range.
- Assign `y` in every arm so the block stays combinational.

#### Notes
Verilog-2001 would write `always @(*)` with an `output reg`. The SystemVerilog version differs in two details that matter on real projects: `always_comb` documents intent to both tools and readers, and an explicit `default` arm means the latch check and the simulation agree even if the select width is later widened.
solution_hints: Map each two-bit select code to its source before typing anything: 00 is a, 01 is b, 10 is c, 11 is d.
Assign y once per arm; four arm assignments plus the default arm is the whole block.
The data inputs never appear in the case expression; only sel is compared.

title: Fix: always_comb Branch That Leaks a Latch
description:
### Problem statement
This selector must output `a` while `en` is high and `b` while `en` is low. The current code handles only the high branch, so when `en` drops the output keeps whatever it held last; the module behaves like a latch and several rows of the test plan fail. Add the missing branch. The grader applies the rows in order and the output value carries over between rows, which is why the stale value is visible in simulation.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_missing_else(
    input  logic       en,
    input  logic [3:0] a,
    input  logic [3:0] b,
    output logic [3:0] y
);
```

#### Requirements
- `y = a` while `en` is 1 and `y = b` while `en` is 0, on every row.
- Add the missing branch inside the existing `always_comb` block; keep the if-else shape.
- After the fix the module must be a pure function of the current inputs.

#### Timing table (first rows)

| en | a | b | y |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | 9 | 5 |
| 0 | 7 | 12 | 12 |
| 1 | 15 | 1 | 15 |
| 0 | 0 | 3 | 3 |

#### Notes
An incomplete if in a procedural block infers a latch in any HDL, but SystemVerilog makes the failure louder: `always_comb` promises the block is combinational, so a latch-inference warning is a contract violation, and tools that would wave it through for `always @(*)` are expected to flag it here. Writing the else arm is the fix; deleting always_comb would only hide the bug.
solution_hints: Trace the broken code row by row: the first en = 0 row keeps the value from the row before it.
Every path through a combinational block must end in an assignment to every output it drives.
One else arm naming b completes the block; no other change is needed.

title: Widen a Nibble with a localparam Pad
description:
### Problem statement
Widen a 4-bit value to a byte two ways: padded above with zeros, and padded above with copies of the sign bit `din[3]`. The pad width is not written as a bare literal; it comes from a `localparam` named `PAD`, so the same constant drives both concatenations and a later width change edits one line.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_widen_localparam(
    input  logic [3:0] din,
    output logic [7:0] zero_ext,
    output logic [7:0] sign_ext
);
```

#### Requirements
- Keep `localparam PAD = 4;` and build both outputs with `{PAD{...}}` replication.
- `zero_ext` is four zero bits above `din`; `sign_ext` is four copies of `din[3]` above `din`.
- Both assignments sit in one `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
The Verilog version of this circuit hard-codes `4'b0000` and `{{4{din[3]}}, din}`. Naming the pad width in a localparam costs nothing at synthesis time but turns a width retarget into a one-line edit, and replication counts driven by constants are checked by the tool instead of by eye.
solution_hints: Concatenation places the padding on the left, since the left operand becomes the most significant bits.
One replication replicates the constant zero, the other replicates the sign bit din[3].
Check din = 8 by hand: the zero path keeps 00001000, the sign path fills the top nibble with ones.

title: BCD Decade Counter with Parallel Load
description:
### Problem statement
Digit counters stop at nine, not at fifteen. Build one in `always_ff`: an asynchronous active-low reset, a `load` input that wins over the enable and forces `count` to `din`, and an enabled increment that wraps from 9 back to 0. The grader drives each row as one clock cycle and samples after the edge; state carries over.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_counter_bcd(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       load,
    input  logic       en,
    input  logic [3:0] din,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears the count immediately and asynchronously.
- `load = 1` at a clock edge loads `din`, whatever `en` is doing.
- With `load = 0` and `en = 1`, the count increments and wraps from 9 to 0; values 10 to 15 never appear.
- With `load = 0` and `en = 0`, the count holds.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | load | en | din | count after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 8 | 8 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 9 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 9 | 9 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

#### Notes
The decade wrap is the one place where a plain `count <= count + 1'b1` is not enough: the four-bit register would run on to 15. Comparing against 9 before incrementing is the standard fix. The `always_ff` keyword is doing the same job as `always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)` here, but it also tells every downstream tool that this block is clocked logic.
solution_hints: Order the branches once and keep them: reset, then load, then enable, then hold.
The wrap test compares the current count against 9 before the increment happens.
Load and enable never mix in one assignment; load is a separate branch that ignores en.

title: Implement the Timing: Gray-Code Sequence Counter
description:
### Problem statement
Two flip-flops whose state walks the Gray sequence 00, 01, 11, 10 change exactly one bit per clock, which is why encoders and CDC FIFO pointers are built this way. Write the `always_ff` block that follows the sequence: each enabled edge advances one step, wrapping from 10 back to 00, and a disabled edge holds. The grader applies one clock cycle per row; state carries over.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_gray_counter(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       en,
    output logic [1:0] count
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `count` to 2'b00 asynchronously.
- On an enabled edge the state advances 00 to 01 to 11 to 10 and back to 00.
- On a disabled edge the state holds.
- A `case` on the current state with a `default` arm is the intended shape.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | en | count after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

#### Notes
Because the sequence is not numeric order, an adder will not generate it; the transition table is the design. This is the same shape an enum FSM takes, with the case labels acting as the state names, and the default arm keeps an impossible encoding from hanging the machine.
solution_hints: Write the four states as a table with the next state in each row before touching the code.
The case arms are 2'b00, 2'b01, 2'b11 and 2'b10; each assigns its successor.
The enable gates the whole case, not individual arms; a disabled edge assigns nothing.

title: Priority Encoder with casez and default
description:
### Problem statement
Interrupt controllers and arbiters need the number of the highest requesting bit, not just any bit. Encode `req[3]` down to `req[0]` with a `casez` pattern match: bit 3 has top priority. `valid` is 0 only when no bit is requested, which is exactly the row the `default` arm covers.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_prio_enc_casez(
    input  logic [3:0] req,
    output logic [2:0] code,
    output logic       valid
);
```

#### Requirements
- One `casez (req)` inside `always_comb`, with pattern arms 4'b1???, 4'b01??, 4'b001? and 4'b0001.
- The matching arm sets `code` to the bit index and `valid` to 1.
- `default` sets `code = 3'd0` and `valid = 1'b0`, and this arm handles the `req = 0` row.

#### Notes
Do not reach for the casez qualifiers that some tools offer: Icarus accepts plain `casez`, and a qualifier adds nothing that the explicit `default` arm does not already guarantee. The request ordering comes from the arm sequence alone, exactly as it does in Verilog; the optional qualifiers are left out of this track because support varies between tools.
solution_hints: The question marks in a casez pattern match either value, so 4'b1??? covers eight requests at once.
Arm order is the priority: put the pattern for bit 3 first and bit 0 last.
The default arm is the only one that sets valid low; every pattern arm claims the bus.

title: Fix: Wrong Enum Literal Jumps the Transition
description:
### Problem statement
This three-state machine walks `S_IDLE`, then `S_RUN` for one cycle when started, then `S_DONE` for one cycle, and returns to idle. It compiles and runs, but starting it skips straight to the done state: the transition out of `S_IDLE` assigns the wrong enum literal. The outputs `busy` and `done` therefore swap their pulses. Repair the one assignment. State carries over between the grader's clock rows.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_enum_transition(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic start,
    output logic busy,
    output logic done
);
```

#### Requirements
- The tour is `S_IDLE` to `S_RUN` on `start`, `S_RUN` to `S_DONE` after one cycle, `S_DONE` to `S_IDLE` after one cycle.
- `busy` is 1 only in `S_RUN`; `done` is 1 only in `S_DONE`.
- Fix the wrong literal in the transition block; change nothing else.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | start | busy | done |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

#### Notes
This is the enum-era version of a wrong localparam in a transition: the literal is spelled correctly and has the right type, so neither the compiler nor the simulator complains. Named states make the bug readable in the source, which is the honest benefit of enums over raw localparams, but they cannot catch a swap between two literals of the same type.
solution_hints: Follow row 2 in the broken code: start from idle lands in the done state, so done pulses where busy should.
The three literals are assigned in two wrong ways and one right way; only the idle transition is broken.
The arm that fires on start must name the running state, not the finished one.

title: Instruction Fields by Bit and Part Select
description:
### Problem statement
Packed instruction words are read by slicing: the top two bits name the operation, the next three the destination register and the low three the source register. Slice them with bit-selects and part-selects on `logic` vectors, one field per output, and verify the boundaries on the ten rows.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_instr_field_select(
    input  logic [7:0] instr,
    output logic [1:0] opcode,
    output logic [2:0] dst,
    output logic [2:0] src
);
```

#### Requirements
- `opcode` is `instr[7:6]`, `dst` is `instr[5:3]`, `src` is `instr[2:0]`.
- The three fields must tile the byte exactly, with no bit used twice and no bit unused.
- Assign all three fields in one `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
Verilog part-selects work the same way on `reg` or `wire`; what SystemVerilog adds here is the guarantee that `logic` ports and variables can be sliced with identical syntax, so the same expressions move freely between a net-driven datapath and a procedural block without re-declaring anything.
solution_hints: Write out the byte as bit positions 7 down to 0 and mark where each field starts and ends.
A two-bit field at the top needs only one part-select; the middle and bottom fields each have their own.
Row 2 is 01010101 in binary: read the three slices off that pattern and check them against the table.

title: Enable-Gated Register in always_ff
description:
### Problem statement
Most registers in a real design do not capture on every clock: an enable decides whether the edge loads new data or the register holds. Build that clock-enable register in `always_ff`, with an asynchronous active-low reset. The grader drives each row as one clock cycle and samples after the edge; the register keeps its value across rows unless the edge loads it.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_ff_enable_hold(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       en,
    input  logic [3:0] d,
    output logic [3:0] q
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `q` to 0 immediately and asynchronously.
- With `en = 1` at a positive edge, `q` captures `d`.
- With `en = 0` at a positive edge, `q` holds its previous value.
- Use one `always_ff` block with nonblocking assignments only.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | en | d | q after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 15 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 5 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 9 | 5 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 9 | 9 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 14 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 14 | 14 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 7 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 7 | 7 |

#### Notes
The `en` branch must assign nothing: writing `q <= q` works but reads like a bug and lints as a redundant capture. Leaving the branch empty is the idiomatic clock-enable, and `always_ff` is what lets the tool confirm that the only assignments in sight are edge-triggered ones.
solution_hints: Two decisions happen per edge, in order: does the reset win, and does the enable open.
The hold case is the absence of an assignment, not an assignment of q to itself.
Rows 3 and 6 are the interesting ones: the edge fires but the enable keeps the old value.

title: Checker: Encodings Outside the Enum Literal Set
description:
### Problem statement
A control bus is supposed to carry one of three commands, but a 2-bit wire can hold four values, and the fourth usually means something upstream is broken. Build the validator: `legal` is 1 for the three encodings the enum declares and 0 for everything else. The enum literals are the case labels and the `default` arm is the rejection path.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_enum_legal(
    input  logic [1:0] state,
    output logic       legal
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, RUN, DONE} ctl_t;` inside the module.
- One `case (state)` inside `always_comb`, with the three enum literals as a grouped arm.
- `default` drives `legal` to 0; every matched literal drives it to 1.

#### Notes
An enum-typed variable can only hold its declared literals, so this checker accepts the raw wire that an enum variable would normally replace. That is the point: at a boundary where untrusted bits arrive, SystemVerilog designers keep the port as `logic` and let the case-plus-default decide legality, because a stray encoding must be detected, not assumed away.
solution_hints: The three literals name encodings 0, 1 and 2; the leftover two-bit value is the only illegal one.
A grouped arm lists labels with commas: one arm can accept all three legal commands.
The default arm is not dead code here; it is the reason the checker exists.

title: Concatenation and Replication on logic Buses
description:
### Problem statement
Three wiring idioms in one module: glue a bus to its complement, tile a bus twice, and fan a single bit out to a nibble. Given `din[3:0]`, drive `joined = {din, ~din}`, `tiled = {2{din}}` and `fan = {4{din[3]}}`, and predict each result on paper before running the rows.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_concat_replicate_bus(
    input  logic [3:0] din,
    output logic [7:0] joined,
    output logic [7:0] tiled,
    output logic [3:0] fan
);
```

#### Requirements
- `joined` places `din` in the high nibble and its complement in the low nibble.
- `tiled` is the input bus written twice, high half first.
- `fan` is four copies of the most significant input bit.
- Assign all three outputs in one `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
Concatenation and replication are the two brace operators, and both predate SystemVerilog; what the `logic` ports change is that the operands can be 4-state variables sliced and recombined without any wire or reg bookkeeping. The classic trap stays the same: the left operand of a concatenation becomes the most significant bits of the result.
solution_hints: For din = 1010, the complement nibble is 0101, so joined is 1010_0101 written as one byte.
Tiling is pure duplication: whatever the four bits are, they appear again immediately to the right.
The fan output only ever reads 0000 or 1111; which one depends solely on din[3].

title: Implement the Timing: Johnson Counter Taps
description:
### Problem statement
A Johnson counter shifts right and feeds the inverted tail back into the top, visiting 2n states before repeating. Starting from the reset value 0000 the taps are 1000, 1100, 1110 and so on. Implement it in `always_ff` and confirm the tour against the table; the grader applies one clock cycle per row and samples after the edge.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_johnson(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    output logic [3:0] q
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `q` to 0000 asynchronously.
- On each positive edge, `q` shifts right one place and `~q[0]` enters as the new bit 3.
- The shift must be one nonblocking assignment using a concatenation.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | q after edge |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 8 |
| 3 | 1 | 12 |
| 4 | 1 | 14 |
| 5 | 1 | 15 |
| 6 | 1 | 7 |
| 7 | 1 | 3 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 8 |

#### Notes
The whole machine is `q <= {~q[0], q[3:1]}`. Reading that line out loud is the design review: the new most significant bit is the inverted old least significant bit, and everything else slides right. Nonblocking assignment is what makes the expression read the old values; the equivalent blocking form would still work here but only by accident of ordering.
solution_hints: Track one bit through the table: it enters inverted at the top and slides to the bottom over four edges.
The concatenation on the right of the nonblocking assignment is built entirely from the old q.
Row 6 is where the first inverted tail arrives at bit 0 and starts turning the ones back into zeros.

title: Three Comparison Flags in One always_comb
description:
### Problem statement
Build the three-flag magnitude comparator for two unsigned 4-bit values in `always_comb`: `gt` when `a` is larger, `lt` when `b` is larger, `eq` on ties, with exactly one flag high for every input pair. The style point is the block: three outputs, one `always_comb`, and assignments ordered so each flag reads as its own question.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_compare_flags_comb(
    input  logic [3:0] a,
    input  logic [3:0] b,
    output logic       gt,
    output logic       eq,
    output logic       lt
);
```

#### Requirements
- Exactly one of `gt`, `eq`, `lt` is 1 for every input pair.
- The values are unsigned; 15 is the largest.
- All three flags are assigned in one `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
In Verilog the same module would declare three `reg` outputs and an `always @(*)` block. With `always_comb` the block promises to re-evaluate on any input change, which removes the stale-flag failure mode where one forgotten sensitivity entry leaves a comparison result frozen from the previous vector.
solution_hints: The equality flag is one comparison; the two inequality flags are two more.
Because exactly one flag may be high, any one flag can be derived as the NOR of the other two.
Verify the boundary rows 0 and 15 before trusting the middle of the range.

title: Fix: Part-Select Nibbles Trade Places
description:
### Problem statement
A byte must be split into nibbles and reassembled with the halves exchanged: `swapped` places the original low nibble above the original high nibble. The current code compiles and produces a plausible byte, but the two part-selects inside the concatenation are written in the wrong order, so `swapped` comes back identical to `din` whenever the halves differ. Repair the one concatenation.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_part_select(
    input  logic [7:0] din,
    output logic [3:0] low4,
    output logic [3:0] high4,
    output logic [7:0] swapped
);
```

#### Requirements
- `low4` is `din[3:0]` and `high4` is `din[7:4]`; both are already correct.
- `swapped` must place the original low nibble in bits 7 to 4 and the original high nibble in bits 3 to 0.
- Fix only the concatenation expression; keep the rest of the module as it is.

#### Timing table (first rows)

| din | low4 | high4 | swapped |
|---|---|---|---|
| 210 | 2 | 13 | 45 |
| 90 | 10 | 5 | 165 |
| 7 | 7 | 0 | 112 |
| 128 | 0 | 8 | 8 |

#### Notes
The bug hides because the concatenation of the two correct slices is still a legal byte: it is just the original one. Part-select syntax in SystemVerilog is the same `[msb:lsb]` form Verilog uses, and the ordering rule inside the braces is also unchanged, which is exactly why this mistake survives review so often.
solution_hints: In the broken code the concatenation reproduces din exactly, so only rows with unequal nibbles can fail.
The left operand of the braces lands on bits 7 to 4; decide which slice belongs there.
Rows 8 and 10 are palindromes where both orders agree, which is why those rows never caught the bug.

title: Binary-Gray Converter Pair in always_comb
description:
### Problem statement
Convert both ways between binary and reflected Gray code, side by side: `gray` from `bin` with the classic shift-and-XOR, and `bcode` from `gryn` by unrolling the same relation from the top bit down. Both conversions live in one `always_comb` block, and every row of the test plan can be double-checked with the round trip.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_gray_pair_convert(
    input  logic [3:0] bin,
    input  logic [3:0] gryn,
    output logic [3:0] gray,
    output logic [3:0] bcode
);
```

#### Requirements
- `gray` is `bin` XORed with itself shifted right by one.
- `bcode` converts `gryn`: the top bit passes through, and each lower bit is the running XOR of the converted bit above it and the Gray bit beside it.
- Both conversions are assigned in one `always_comb` block; the two inputs are independent.

#### Notes
The forward direction is one expression; the reverse is a chain, because each binary bit depends on the one above it. Writing both in `always_comb` keeps the two directions visually parallel, and the intermediate chain can use local `logic` variables declared in the module instead of the wire declarations the Verilog version would need.
solution_hints: Forward first: each gray bit is the XOR of the matching and the next-higher binary bit, with bit 3 passing through.
Reverse by unrolling from the top: recover one binary bit, then use it to recover the next one down.
Check every row by converting your bcode back to gray; it must reproduce the gryn you were given.

title: Swap Nibbles Through a packed struct
description:
### Problem statement
Move a byte through a `typedef struct packed` view of itself: unpack `d` into a struct with `hi` and `lo` fields, copy the fields into a second struct the other way around, and pack the result out as `swapped`. The field-order rule of packed structs is the actual lesson: the first declared field occupies the most significant bits.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_struct_nibble_swap(
    input  logic [7:0] d,
    output logic [3:0] hi_in,
    output logic [3:0] lo_in,
    output logic [7:0] swapped
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef struct packed { logic [3:0] hi; logic [3:0] lo; } byte_split_t;` with two instances, one per stage.
- `hi_in` and `lo_in` report the unpacked input nibbles: `d[7:4]` and `d[3:0]`.
- `swapped` is the second struct packed back out, with the fields exchanged.
- All assignments live in one `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
A packed struct is a vector wearing names: `{hi, lo}` in declaration order means `hi` owns bits 7 to 4. That makes the field list a replacement for hand-written part-selects, and the swap becomes two named assignments instead of two magic slices. Verilog-2001 has no struct, so the same circuit is written with bare `[7:4]` and `[3:0]` expressions and a comment to say which is which.
solution_hints: Stage one fills in_s: the hi field takes d[7:4] and the lo field takes d[3:0].
Stage two copies across the fields in crossed order, then packs out_s back into a byte.
Row 4 is 00010010: the fields are 1 and 2, so the swap must read 2 and then 1, byte value 33.

title: Implement the Timing: start and done Drive a Busy Flag
description:
### Problem statement
A one-bit status flag is the smallest handshake block: `start` sets `busy`, `done` clears it, and when both arrive in the same cycle `done` wins. Write the `always_ff` block that produces the table, then trace rows 8 and 9 by hand until the priority is obvious. The grader applies one clock cycle per row; the flag carries over.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_busy_flag(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic start,
    input  logic done,
    output logic busy
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `busy` asynchronously.
- At a positive edge with `rst_n` high, `busy` becomes 1 when `start` is high and `done` low, and 0 when `done` is high.
- With both inputs low, `busy` holds.
- One nonblocking assignment with boolean operators covers the whole behaviour.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | start | done | busy after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

#### Notes
The whole block is `busy <= (busy | start) & ~done`. Building it from a set-and-clear pair first, then merging, is the same exercise a Verilog designer would do; SystemVerilog only changes the wrapper, and `always_ff` is what tells the synthesis tool this single line is a register with feedback rather than a mislabelled latch.
solution_hints: Write the truth table for busy as a function of busy, start and done before writing any Verilog.
The set term is the old busy OR start; the clear term is done, and it must win the fight.
Row 8 is the priority witness: start and done together leave the flag low.

title: Bundle an Adder Result in a packed struct
description:
### Problem statement
Adders carry more than a sum: the carry-out and a zero flag travel with it through every datapath stage. Declare a `typedef struct packed` result type holding `sum`, `carry` and `zero`, fill one instance in `always_comb`, and unpack its fields onto the three outputs. The struct is the internal currency; the ports stay plain.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_struct_alu_flags(
    input  logic [3:0] a,
    input  logic [3:0] b,
    output logic [3:0] sum,
    output logic       carry,
    output logic       zero
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef struct packed { logic [3:0] sum; logic carry; logic zero; } add_result_t;` and one instance `res`.
- Compute a 5-bit total from `a`, `b` and no carry-in; the top bit is `carry`, the low four are `sum`.
- `zero` is 1 exactly when the 4-bit sum is 0000, including the true wrap cases.
- Unpack the struct fields onto the outputs in the same `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
Grouping results in a struct is how SystemVerilog keeps a datapath stage's outputs from sprawling into a dozen ports: one type, one bundle, assigned field by field. Verilog-2001 would pass the same three values as separate signals with naming conventions doing the grouping by hand.
solution_hints: Widen first: two 4-bit operands added into a 5-bit intermediate keep the carry from vanishing.
The struct fields take the pieces in declaration order: sum, then carry, then zero.
Zero is a property of the 4-bit result, so a carry that wraps to 0000 still sets it.

title: One-Hot Builder with a Full case
description:
### Problem statement
Turn a 3-bit select into an 8-bit one-hot word where only bit `sel` is set. All eight select values get their own `case` arm in `always_comb`, and a `default` arm rides along so the block stays complete if the select width ever grows. This is the encoder's mirror image, and it is where arm-per-value style starts to beat shifting.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_onehot_build_case(
    input  logic [2:0] sel,
    output logic [7:0] oh
);
```

#### Requirements
- One `case (sel)` inside `always_comb` with eight explicit arms, `3'd0` through `3'd7`.
- Arm n drives `oh` with bit n set and all other bits clear.
- Include `default: oh = 8'h00;` after the eight arms.

#### Notes
A shift expression `8'h01 << sel` builds the same word in one line, and either answer is acceptable hardware. The case version is the one that scales to irregular patterns, such as decoders with gaps or priority masks, and writing all eight arms plus a default is the drill that keeps those bigger tables honest.
solution_hints: Each arm assigns one 8-bit literal; write them all out rather than trying to compute the pattern.
The bit that is set sits at the position named by the select value, counting from bit 0.
The default arm mirrors the all-clear word and never fires for a 3-bit select, but it completes the table.

title: Fix: Replication Count Drops a Bit
description:
### Problem statement
The zero-extend path in this widener is correct, but the sign-extend path was edited and its replication count now says 3 instead of 4. The result is a 7-bit value that quietly zero-pads into the 8-bit output, so every negative-looking nibble reads wrong. Repair the count, ideally by reusing the `PAD` localparam so the two paths cannot drift apart again.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_replicate(
    input  logic [3:0] din,
    output logic [7:0] zero_ext,
    output logic [7:0] sign_ext
);
```

#### Requirements
- `zero_ext` is four zero bits above `din` and already passes.
- `sign_ext` must be four copies of `din[3]` above `din`.
- Fix the replication count; using the existing `PAD` constant is the preferred form.

#### Timing table (first rows)

| din | zero_ext | sign_ext |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 8 | 248 |
| 15 | 15 | 255 |
| 5 | 5 | 5 |
| 12 | 12 | 252 |

#### Notes
A replication count that is one too small does not raise a width error here: Verilog and SystemVerilog both zero-extend the short result into the assignment target. The bug is only visible as wrong values, which is why the test plan leans on rows where `din[3]` is 1. Tying the count to a localparam makes the failure impossible to reintroduce.
solution_hints: Count the bits in the broken expression: three sign copies plus the four data bits make seven, not eight.
The localparam named PAD is already in the file and already used by the passing path.
Rows where din[3] is 0 pass by accident; check din = 8 to see the defect.

title: Two-to-Four Decoder with always_comb and default
description:
### Problem statement
Decode a 2-bit address into a one-hot select line, gated by an enable: with `en` high exactly one output bit matches the address, and with `en` low the whole output word is zero. The recommended shape assigns a default low word first, then switches on the address inside `always_comb`, so every path leaves the outputs fully assigned.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_decoder2to4_comb(
    input  logic [1:0] a,
    input  logic       en,
    output logic [3:0] y
);
```

#### Requirements
- With `en = 1`, exactly one bit of `y` is high: bit `a`, with the rest low.
- With `en = 0`, all four bits of `y` are 0 regardless of the address.
- Use `always_comb` with a default assignment or a default case arm; no output path may be unassigned.

#### Notes
This is the module where the default-first style pays for itself: assign `y = 4'b0000` unconditionally, then overwrite one bit in the case arms. That structure is latch-free by construction, and `always_comb` backs the promise by inferring the sensitivity list instead of trusting the designer's `always @(*)`.
solution_hints: A one-hot word for address n has exactly bit n set; write the four literals and check them in binary.
The enable can gate the whole decode with one if, or fold into each arm; the first is shorter.
The default low assignment before the case is what lets the disabled rows stay all-zero.

title: Implement the Timing: Down Counter Through Zero
description:
### Problem statement
Baud generators and timer loads often count down, and the interesting cycle is the one where 0 wraps to 15 in a 4-bit register. Build the down counter in `always_ff`: reset clears to 0, an enabled edge decrements, a disabled edge holds, and the wrap is free arithmetic rather than a special case. The grader applies one clock cycle per row.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_wrap_counter(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       en,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `count` to 0 asynchronously.
- With `en = 1` at a positive edge, `count` decrements by one, wrapping from 0 to 15.
- With `en = 0`, `count` holds.
- One nonblocking decrement covers the whole behaviour; no special wrap logic.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | en | count after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 15 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 14 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 13 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 13 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 12 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 11 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 10 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 9 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 8 |

#### Notes
The 4-bit decrement does the wrap by itself: 0000 minus 1 is 1111. Adding an explicit comparison would work but trains the wrong instinct for wider counters with modulus bounds. `always_ff` plus one arithmetic nonblocking assignment is the complete design.
solution_hints: Row 2 is the whole point: the register holds 0000 and the decrement lands on 1111.
The enable gates the decrement exactly as it gated the increment in the up-counter exercise.
A disabled edge assigns nothing; resist writing count <= count - 1'b0.

title: Enum Opcode Labels in an ALU case
description:
### Problem statement
A 2-bit opcode field selects one of four operations on two 4-bit operands: add, subtract, bitwise AND and bitwise OR. The opcodes are declared as `typedef enum logic [1:0] {OP_ADD, OP_SUB, OP_AND, OP_OR} opcode_t;` inside the module, and the literals stand in for the bare numbers as the `case` labels in `always_comb`.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_alu_enum_opcode(
    input  logic [3:0] a,
    input  logic [3:0] b,
    input  logic [1:0] op_in,
    output logic [3:0] y
);
```

#### Requirements
- Keep the `opcode_t` typedef exactly as given and use its literals as the case labels.
- `OP_ADD` drives `a + b`, `OP_SUB` drives `a - b`, `OP_AND` drives `a & b`, `OP_OR` drives `a | b`, all truncated to 4 bits.
- Include a `default` arm that drives `y` to zero.
- The literal encodings are declaration order: OP_ADD is 0, OP_SUB is 1, OP_AND is 2, OP_OR is 3.

#### Notes
The case expression stays the raw `op_in` port and the labels are the enum literals, which is the safe way to mix a typed vocabulary with an untyped boundary. Casting the port into an enum variable is the fuller SystemVerilog treatment, but it needs a static cast and out-of-range values become undefined behaviour; the case-literal form keeps every possible input defined.
solution_hints: Four arms and a default; each arm is a single assignment with one operator.
Row 9 is the subtraction that borrows: 3 minus 9 wraps inside the 4-bit result.
The enum literals are constants; the case expression itself remains the plain port.

title: Checker: One-Hot Grant on a logic Vector
description:
### Problem statement
Arbiters promise one-hot grants, and a checker is what holds them to it across an 8-bit bus. `ok` must be 1 exactly when precisely one bit of `grant` is set: not the all-zero word, not any multi-hot pattern. The subtract trick does the heavy lifting inside one `always_comb` block.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_onehot_8bit(
    input  logic [7:0] grant,
    output logic       ok
);
```

#### Requirements
- `ok` is 1 exactly for the eight one-hot values: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128.
- `ok` is 0 for 0 and for every multi-hot word.
- One `always_comb` block; the power-of-two test plus a nonzero test is the intended form.

#### Notes
`grant & (grant - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so it lands on zero only for powers of two, and the zero word has to be excluded separately because the trick accepts it. SystemVerilog's contribution here is comfort, not novelty: the whole checker is two boolean terms on `logic` operands in an `always_comb` block that no longer needs a hand-maintained sensitivity list.
solution_hints: Two failure families must both drive ok low: the empty bus and the crowded bus.
Subtracting one from a power of two flips that bit and every zero below it, leaving nothing in common with the original.
Combine the power-of-two test with an explicit nonzero test; neither term alone is sufficient.

title: D Latch with always_latch
description:
### Problem statement
Build a level-sensitive D latch: while `en` is high the output follows `d`, and while `en` is low the last captured value is held. SystemVerilog has a block kind for exactly this shape, `always_latch`, and the test plan exercises the transparent and holding phases in sequence; each row is one stimulus vector and `q` carries over between rows.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_d_latch_en(
    input  logic en,
    input  logic d,
    output logic q
);
```

#### Requirements
- While `en = 1`, `q` equals `d`.
- While `en = 0`, `q` holds its last captured value.
- Use `always_latch` with a blocking assignment and an if on `en`.

#### Timing table (stimulus rows in order)

| row | en | d | q after row |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 7 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

#### Notes
`always_latch` is the third procedural block kind alongside `always_comb` and `always_ff`, and it is honest about producing a memory element instead of pretending to be combinational. The Verilog version writes `always @*` and lets the incomplete if silently imply the latch; the SystemVerilog keyword declares that the latch is the intent, which also keeps lint tools from flagging a deliberate design.
solution_hints: The block fires whenever en or d changes, but only the en = 1 rows assign q.
Rows 3, 4, 7 and 9 are hold rows: d moves under the latch and the output must not care.
One if with one assignment is the entire body; there is no else to write.

title: Fix: casez Encoder Holds a Stale Code
description:
### Problem statement
This priority encoder has four pattern arms for the four possible request positions, but the all-zero bus matches none of them, so `code` and `valid` keep their previous values instead of reporting an idle bus. The test plan catches it: any row with `req = 0` after a request keeps the stale encoding. Add the missing `default` arm.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_casez_default(
    input  logic [3:0] req,
    output logic [2:0] code,
    output logic       valid
);
```

#### Requirements
- Every arm keeps its current pattern and values.
- Add a `default` arm that drives `code = 3'd0` and `valid = 1'b0`.
- The `req = 0` rows must report the idle encoding, not a leftover one.

#### Timing table (first rows)

| req | code | valid |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 3 | 1 |
| 4 | 2 | 1 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |

#### Notes
The four pattern arms look like they cover the bus, and for every nonzero request they do. The gap is the encodings that match no pattern, and only the explicit `default` arm closes it. This is the same lesson the `always_comb` latch warning teaches: an unassigned path in a combinational block is a memory, and a checker built from this encoder would inherit the stale verdict.
starter_code:
module sv_fix_casez_default(
    input  logic [3:0] req,
    output logic [2:0] code,
    output logic       valid
);
    always_comb begin
        casez (req)
            4'b1???: begin code = 3'd3; valid = 1'b1; end
            4'b01??: begin code = 3'd2; valid = 1'b1; end
            4'b001?: begin code = 3'd1; valid = 1'b1; end
            4'b0001: begin code = 3'd0; valid = 1'b1; end
        endcase
    end
endmodule
solution_hints: Row 3 is the tell: req drops to zero right after two requests, and the broken code repeats the last code.
The pattern arms stay untouched; only one new arm is added at the end of the casez.
The default arm must assign both outputs, since both are currently left unassigned on that path.

title: Two-Request Enum FSM with Stop Priority
description:
### Problem statement
A motor controller has two request lines: `run_req` starts the machine and `stop_req` halts it, and when both assert in the same cycle the stop must win for safety. The states are `typedef enum logic [1:0] {S_STOP, S_RUN} state_t` literals, the transitions are an if-else chain in `always_ff`, and `running` is a state comparison in `always_comb`. Trace the priority rows before coding.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fsm_stop_run(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic run_req,
    input  logic stop_req,
    output logic running
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n` asynchronously returns the machine to `S_STOP`.
- `stop_req = 1` forces `S_STOP` on the next edge, even when `run_req` is also high.
- Otherwise `run_req = 1` moves to `S_RUN`; with both requests low the state holds.
- `running` is 1 exactly in `S_RUN`.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | run_req | stop_req | running after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

#### Notes
The stop-wins rule is one if-else ordering decision, and the enum does not change that: what the typedef changes is that `S_STOP` and `S_RUN` are typed names instead of localparam numbers, so the comparison in the output block reads as intent. The two-request structure also differs from the single-input machine in this track on purpose; sequencing requests is where state machines start earning their keep.
solution_hints: Write the request pairs as a mini truth table: 11 goes to stop, 10 to run, 01 to stop, 00 holds.
The if-else chain encodes the priority directly: stop checked first, run second, nothing for hold.
Rows 5 and 7 are the priority witnesses; run_req is high there but must lose.

title: Implement the Timing: Enum Tour with Illegal-State Recovery
description:
### Problem statement
This machine declares three enum states but its register is a raw 3-bit vector, so the arithmetic transition out of `S_DONE` can walk the encoding one step past the literal set, into a value no literal names. The `err` output must flag that cycle, and the `default` arm must return the machine to `S_IDLE` on the next tick. Implement the block so the table holds.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_fsm_tour(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic tick,
    output logic done_led,
    output logic err
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef enum logic [2:0] {S_IDLE, S_STEP, S_DONE} state_t;` inside the module and hold the state in `logic [2:0] state`.
- On each ticked edge: `S_IDLE` goes to `S_STEP`, `S_STEP` goes to `S_DONE`, `S_DONE` adds one to the raw encoding, and `default` returns to `S_IDLE`.
- `done_led` is 1 exactly in the `S_DONE` encoding; `err` is 1 exactly when the state matches none of the three literals.
- A disabled edge holds the state.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | tick | done_led | err |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

#### Notes
An enum-typed state variable cannot legally hold an unnamed encoding, but a raw vector can, and real designs mix both: the literals give readable labels while the vector admits arithmetic transitions. The pairing of an `err` flag with a `default` recovery arm is the standard defensive answer, and the table shows the illegal encoding surviving exactly one held cycle before the next tick repairs it.
solution_hints: Number the encodings: the literals are 0, 1 and 2, so adding one in the done state lands on 3.
The err expression has three negated comparisons ANDed together; it is the exact complement of the case labels.
Row 9 holds the illegal encoding because the tick is low; recovery waits for the next tick.

title: Reduction XOR Parity in always_comb
description:
### Problem statement
Count ones without counting: the XOR-reduction of `data` is 1 exactly when the byte holds an odd number of ones. Drive the `odd` output with that single reduction inside `always_comb`, and use the ten rows to confirm the result on bytes with 0 through 8 ones.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_parity_always_comb(
    input  logic [7:0] data,
    output logic       odd
);
```

#### Requirements
- `odd` is 1 for 1, 3, 5 or 7 ones in `data`, and 0 for 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 ones.
- One reduction expression assigned in one `always_comb` block.
- No loops and no intermediate variables.

#### Notes
The reduction operator is identical in Verilog and SystemVerilog; the difference is the habitat. In Verilog the natural home is an `assign` onto a wire; here it is an `always_comb` onto an `output logic`, the same block style the rest of the track uses, so parity trees and checker outputs share one idiom.
solution_hints: The prefix operator sits alone before the operand; there is no right-hand argument to write.
Spot-check three rows: 128 has one one, 170 has four, 255 has eight.
The output answers oddness, not evenness; the two differ by one inversion.

title: Fix: Blocking Assignments in an always_ff Stage
description:
### Problem statement
This two-stage delay line must output `sin` on `q` one cycle later and on `dly` two cycles later. The code compiles, but `dly` tracks `sin` with only one cycle of delay: the two assignments in the sequential block use blocking `=`, so the second statement reads the already-updated `q`. Convert the block to nonblocking assignments and the pipeline deepens back to two stages.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_ff_blocking(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic sin,
    output logic q,
    output logic dly
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears both `q` and `dly` asynchronously.
- At each positive edge with `rst_n` high, `q` takes the old `sin` path and `dly` takes the old `q`.
- Change the assignment operators inside the block; keep the statement order and the reset.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | sin | q | dly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

#### Notes
With blocking assignments, `q = sin; dly = q;` executes top to bottom inside one evaluation, so `dly` samples the new `q` and the second stage vanishes. Nonblocking `<=` schedules both updates from the pre-edge values, which is what a pipeline means. Icarus does not police the operator inside `always_ff`; the test rows do.
solution_hints: Trace the broken code at row 2: q and dly both come out 1, so the second stage carried nothing.
The reset branch has the same defect; both operators in both branches must change.
After the fix, dly at each row equals q from the row before, and q equals sin from the row before.

title: One-to-Four Demux with a Data Line
description:
### Problem statement
A decoder picks a wire; a demux routes data onto it. With `en` high, `d` must appear on output bit `sel` and nowhere else; with `en` low, or `d` low, every output is 0. Build it in `always_comb` with a default-zero word first, then a case that writes exactly one bit.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_demux2to4_comb(
    input  logic       d,
    input  logic       en,
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    output logic [3:0] y
);
```

#### Requirements
- `en = 1` and `d = 1` set exactly bit `sel` of `y` and clear the rest.
- `en = 0` or `d = 0` drive all four bits low, whatever `sel` holds.
- Assign a default all-zero word, then write one bit in each case arm.
- Bit-indexed writes like `y[0] = d` inside the arms are the intended style.

#### Notes
The demux is the decoder plus one data term, and the default-first structure carries over unchanged: clear the whole word, then overwrite one element. Writing `y[sel] = d` with a variable index also works, but the case form keeps every routed bit visible in the source, which is the habit this exercise installs.
solution_hints: Clear the whole word once at the top of the block; the case arms then only ever set one bit.
The enable decides whether any bit is written at all; the data value decides what is written.
Rows 5 and 6 separate the two silence conditions: disabled cell and zero data.

title: Hex Digit to Seven-Segment with case
description:
### Problem statement
Render a hex nibble on seven segments: bit 6 of `seg` drives segment a (top), bit 5 is b, and so on down to bit 0 for the middle bar g. All sixteen digits get an explicit case arm in `always_comb`, with a dark default arm after them. The table below gives the exact encodings to hit.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_hex7seg_case(
    input  logic [3:0] nib,
    output logic [6:0] seg
);
```

#### Requirements
- Segment order in `seg` is a, b, c, d, e, f, g from bit 6 down to bit 0; a lit segment is a 1.
- Digit encodings: 0 is 126, 1 is 48, 2 is 109, 3 is 121, 4 is 51, 5 is 91, 6 is 95, 7 is 112.
- Letter encodings: A is 119, b is 31, C is 78, d is 61, E is 79, F is 71; 8 is 127 and 9 is 123.
- The `default` arm drives `seg` to 7'b0000000.

#### Notes
Sixteen arms is where case style starts to look long, and the temptation is a shift or a lookup; the case version is still the one that survives a segment-map change with the least collateral damage. The module also shows the port-width habit of this track: `output logic [6:0]` driven from `always_comb`, replacing the Verilog `output reg [6:0]` pair.
solution_hints: Translate the decimal encodings to binary before writing the arms; each bit is one segment.
Digit 0 lights everything except the middle bar, which is why its encoding is one below 127.
Write the sixteen arms in numeric order and let the default arm stay dark for unreachable codes.

title: Checker: Adjacent Gray Codes
description:
### Problem statement
FIFO pointers travel as Gray codes so that a sampling clock never sees more than one bit move. This checker watches two 4-bit codes and asserts `adjacent` only when they differ in exactly one bit position and are not equal. A `casez` on the XOR of the two codes expresses the whole rule in four pattern arms and a default.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_gray_adjacent(
    input  logic [3:0] code_a,
    input  logic [3:0] code_b,
    output logic       adjacent
);
```

#### Requirements
- `adjacent` is 1 exactly when `code_a ^ code_b` is one of 0001, 0010, 0100 and 1000.
- Equal codes are not adjacent; the all-zero difference falls to `default`.
- One `casez` inside `always_comb` with a `default` arm is the intended structure.

#### Notes
The casez patterns match the four single-bit differences directly, and every multi-bit difference lands in `default`. Verilog would express the same rule with an AND-mask expression; the casez form trades arithmetic cleverness for a table that can be read arm by arm, which is usually the better trade inside a checker.
solution_hints: The XOR word is the only thing the casez sees; each arm names one single-bit pattern.
The equal-codes row produces an all-zero XOR and must fall to default, not to an arm.
Row 4 differs in all four bits, which is the extreme case of the not-adjacent family.

title: Shift Register with Parallel Load
description:
### Problem statement
Serializers warm up by loading a parallel word, then clock it out one bit at a time. Build that register in `always_ff`: `load` forces `q` to `din` on the edge, otherwise `q` shifts left with `sin` entering at bit 0, and the asynchronous active-low reset clears everything. The grader applies one clock cycle per row.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_shift_load_4bit(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       load,
    input  logic       sin,
    input  logic [3:0] din,
    output logic [3:0] q
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `q` asynchronously.
- `load = 1` at a positive edge loads `din`, ignoring `sin`.
- With `load = 0`, each positive edge shifts `q` one place left with `sin` entering bit 0.
- One `always_ff` block; the shift is a concatenation `{q[2:0], sin}`.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | load | sin | din | q after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 9 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 9 | 9 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 3 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 6 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 13 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 7 | 7 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 15 |
| 8 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 14 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 12 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 9 |

#### Notes
The load-versus-shift decision is one if-else in the clocked block, and the shift itself is a concatenation rather than an operator chain. Declaring the port `output logic [3:0]` and driving it from `always_ff` is the SystemVerilog pattern; the Verilog template would declare `output reg [3:0]` and mean the same thing with older vocabulary.
solution_hints: The branch order is reset, then load, then shift; each later branch can assume the earlier ones failed.
Shifting left with sin at the bottom is {q[2:0], sin}; the top bit of the old q falls off.
Rows 7 to 10 shift a loaded 7 through four serial bits; follow one bit across the rows.

title: Fix: Output case Misses an Enum State
description:
### Problem statement
The machine in this exercise visits three states in a loop, and the output rule is: `y` is 1 in `S_A` and `S_C`, 0 in `S_B`. The output block's `case` covers only two of the three states, so whenever the machine sits in `S_C` the output freezes at its previous value instead of returning to 1. Add the missing arm. State carries over between the grader's clock rows.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_case_arm(
    input  logic clk,
    input  logic rst_n,
    input  logic adv,
    output logic y
);
```

#### Requirements
- The state machine cycles `S_A`, `S_B`, `S_C`, back to `S_A` on each `adv` edge; that block is already correct.
- `y` must be 1 in `S_A`, 0 in `S_B` and 1 in `S_C`.
- Add the missing arm to the output `case`; change nothing else.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | adv | y after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 1 |

#### Notes
The transition case has a `default` arm and the output case does not, and only the output case is broken. SystemVerilog tools treat a missing arm in `always_comb` as a latch risk, because the case expression can legally name a value no arm matches; an enum-typed case expression narrows that set to the declared literals, which makes the missing arm easy to spot but no less real in simulation.
solution_hints: Trace the broken code into row 3: the machine reaches S_C and y stops following the state.
The output rule needs one more arm than the case currently has; the value there is the same as in S_A.
The transition block already handles all three states plus default; it is not the bug.

title: Implement the Timing: Serial Pattern Through the Register
description:
### Problem statement
Serial receivers reconstruct a parallel word one bit per clock, and reading the half-filled register is the standard way to debug the stream. Build the 4-bit shift register in `always_ff` and trace the pattern through it: each enabled edge shifts left with `sin` entering bit 0. The grader applies one clock cycle per row and samples after the edge.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_shift_pattern(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       sin,
    output logic [3:0] q
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `q` asynchronously.
- Each positive edge with `rst_n` high shifts `q` left one place, with `sin` entering bit 0.
- One nonblocking concatenation assignment in one `always_ff` block.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | sin | q after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 6 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 13 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 10 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 4 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 9 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 6 |

#### Notes
Row 6 is where the first captured bit falls off the top of the register, and the table keeps going long enough to show it. The shift is `q <= {q[2:0], sin}`; `always_ff` is the label that says this concatenation feeds a register rather than combinational logic, and the nonblocking operator is what lets the expression read the old `q` cleanly.
solution_hints: Track the newest bit at the bottom and the oldest at the top; four clocks is a full refresh.
Row 5 shifts a 0110 left with a 1 entering: 1101, which is 13.
After row 6 the bit captured at row 2 has left the register; check that your trace agrees.

title: Checker: Range Guard with localparam Bounds
description:
### Problem statement
A parameterised checker beats three copies of the same comparisons. `val` is legal on the inclusive range 12 to 45, and the bounds live in two `localparam`s. Drive `below` and `above` from the two boundary tests, and derive `in_range` so that exactly one of the three flags is high for every value.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_range_guard(
    input  logic [5:0] val,
    output logic       below,
    output logic       above,
    output logic       in_range
);
```

#### Requirements
- Keep `localparam LOW = 12;` and `localparam HIGH = 45;` and test against those names.
- `below` is 1 when `val` is under 12; `above` is 1 when `val` is over 45.
- `in_range` is 1 exactly on the inclusive range, and the three flags never overlap.
- All three outputs are assigned in one `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
The interesting rows are the boundaries: 11 and 46 fail, 12 and 45 pass. Naming the bounds in `localparam`s means a retarget edits two lines and the boundary rows stay as the regression test, which is the SystemVerilog refinement over the Verilog version's hard-coded magic numbers.
solution_hints: Two comparisons decide everything: one against LOW and one against HIGH.
In_range is the neither-failure case, so it can be the NOR of the other two flags.
Rows 3 and 4 sit exactly on the boundaries; strict and non-strict comparisons must not be mixed up.

title: Counter with a Registered Wrap Flag
description:
### Problem statement
Downstream logic rarely watches a counter directly; it wants a pulse that says a wrap just happened. Build a 3-bit enabled counter whose `wrap` output is a register: at the edge where the count moves from 7 to 0, `wrap` captures 1 and holds it for exactly that one cycle. The grader applies one clock cycle per row; both outputs carry over.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_counter_wrap_flag(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic       en,
    output logic [2:0] count,
    output logic       wrap
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `count` and `wrap` asynchronously.
- With `en = 1` at a positive edge, `count` increments with 3-bit wrap, and `wrap` captures whether the old count was 7.
- With `en = 0`, both `count` and `wrap` hold.
- `wrap` must be registered, not combinational: it is high the cycle after the 7-to-0 edge.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | en | count after edge | wrap after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 4 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 6 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 7 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 7 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |

#### Notes
The flag is registered from the pre-edge count, which puts the pulse one cycle after the arithmetic wrap; a combinational `wrap` on the rolled-over count would miss the row the consumer cares about. Both registers live in the same `always_ff`, which is the SystemVerilog arrangement for related state that must update together.
solution_hints: The wrap capture compares the count before the edge, so the test and the increment share one always_ff row.
Row 9 is the trap: the count sits at 7 with the enable low, and the flag must still be 0.
Row 10 is where the old count of 7 finally meets an enabled edge and the flag captures 1.

title: Fix: One logic Variable with Two Drivers
description:
### Problem statement
This module is supposed to output the bitwise OR of `a` and `b`, but `y` is written twice: once by a continuous assignment and once by an `always_comb` block. A `logic` variable is allowed exactly one driver, so the grader cannot even elaborate this file. Keep the OR as the specification, delete the wrong driver, and the module compiles and passes.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_two_drivers(
    input  logic [3:0] a,
    input  logic [3:0] b,
    output logic [3:0] y
);
```

#### Requirements
- `y` must equal `a | b` on every row.
- Exactly one driver may remain on `y`: either the assign or the always_comb, not both.
- Keep the port list unchanged.

#### Timing table (first rows)

| a | b | y |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 3 | 7 |
| 8 | 4 | 12 |
| 0 | 9 | 9 |
| 15 | 15 | 15 |

#### Notes
Verilog enforced the same rule differently: a `reg` could not take a continuous assignment at all, so the conflict was caught by the declaration. SystemVerilog's `logic` accepts either driver style, which is more flexible and also easier to break; two drivers on one variable is an elaboration error, not a warning, and the fix is to choose one style per signal.
solution_hints: Count the assignment statements that name y; the specification needs exactly one.
If you keep the always_comb block, its expression must be the OR the specification asks for.
Rows 9 and 10 are cheap checks: 1 OR 1 is 1 and 14 OR 1 is 15 under the OR spec.

title: Implement the Timing: Two-Stage struct Pipeline
description:
### Problem statement
A two-stage pipeline hand-carries an operand pair: stage 1 registers `in_a` and `in_b` together in a packed struct, stage 2 registers their sum. The result therefore trails the input by two cycles, and the table is the proof. Declare the struct, build the two register stages in one `always_ff`, and trace the table by hand.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_trace_struct_pipeline(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic [3:0] in_a,
    input  logic [3:0] in_b,
    output logic [4:0] sum
);
```

#### Requirements
- Declare `typedef struct packed { logic [3:0] a; logic [3:0] b; } operand_t;` with one instance `s1` for stage 1.
- `rst_n = 0` clears `s1` and `sum` asynchronously.
- Each positive edge registers the input pair into `s1` and computes `sum` from the previous `s1`, so the sum trails the input by two edges.
- `sum` is 5 bits, so a 15 plus 1 arriving at stage 2 reads 16.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | in_a | in_b | sum after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 3 | 4 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 7 |
| 4 | 1 | 9 | 2 | 2 |
| 5 | 1 | 5 | 6 | 11 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 11 |
| 7 | 1 | 15 | 1 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 16 |
| 9 | 1 | 7 | 7 | 4 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 14 |

#### Notes
The struct is the payload that crosses the stage boundary, which keeps the two operands from drifting apart or being sampled from different cycles. Registering straight into the output port `sum` is the stage-2 register, and `always_ff` covers both stages in one block: two nonblocking assignments per edge, each reading only the pre-edge values.
solution_hints: Row 3 is the first visible result: the pair loaded in row 2 reaches stage 2 and sums to 7.
The 5-bit output matters at row 8, where the row-7 pair of 15 and 1 must read 16.
Each edge does two things at once: load the new pair, and add the old pair.

title: Checker: Data Holds Until Enable Opens
description:
### Problem statement
A capture window closes while `en` is low, so whatever `cap` held at that moment must still be on `cur`: any drift means something upstream wrote through a closed window. The checker raises `stable_ok` whenever `en` is high, because the window is open and movement is allowed, and otherwise demands `cur == cap`.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_stable_en(
    input  logic       en,
    input  logic [3:0] cap,
    input  logic [3:0] cur,
    output logic       stable_ok
);
```

#### Requirements
- With `en = 0`, `stable_ok` is 1 exactly when `cur` equals `cap`.
- With `en = 1`, `stable_ok` is 1 regardless of the data.
- One expression or one if-else in a single `always_comb` block.

#### Notes
The enable term does the gating, and the equality term does the checking; OR-ing them is the whole design. This shape, a condition that switches a checker between watching and tolerating, is the combinational seed of the SystemVerilog stability checks, here written out longhand because this track stays inside synthesizable always blocks.
solution_hints: Two questions decide the output: is the window open, and does the data still match.
Row 6 is the tolerance case: with the window open, any cur is acceptable.
The checker never compares cur against anything but cap; there is no history to store.

title: Fix: Reset Polarity Inverted in always_ff
description:
### Problem statement
This register is specified with an asynchronous active-low reset: `rst_n = 0` clears `q` immediately, and normal operation happens with `rst_n` high. The code has the polarity backwards, so it clears the register on every normal edge and loads data only while the reset is asserted. Nearly every row of the test plan fails. Correct the condition inside the block.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_fix_rst_polarity(
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       rst_n,
    input  logic [3:0] d,
    output logic [3:0] q
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n = 0` clears `q` to 0 immediately and asynchronously.
- With `rst_n = 1` at a positive edge, `q` captures `d`.
- Fix the reset condition inside the always_ff block; keep the sensitivity list and the structure.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | d | q after edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 9 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 5 | 5 |
| 3 | 1 | 12 | 12 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 15 | 15 |
| 6 | 1 | 7 | 7 |
| 7 | 0 | 3 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 10 | 10 |
| 9 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 10 | 0 | 14 | 0 |

#### Notes
The sensitivity list already says `negedge rst_n`, which promises an active-low asynchronous reset, and the body must agree with it. In Verilog the mismatch is just as easy to write and just as silent; SystemVerilog's `always_ff` label does not check polarity either, which is why reset polarity belongs on every review checklist next to the sensitivity list itself.
solution_hints: Trace row 2 in the broken code: the reset is released but the register clears anyway.
The condition and the sensitivity list must describe the same reset; one of them is inverted.
Only the if condition changes; both branches keep their assignments.

title: BCD Digit Increment with an Invalid Guard
description:
### Problem statement
One step of a decimal counter, as a combinational service: `inc` is the digit after `bcd`, `carry` fires only when 9 rolls to 0, and inputs above 9 are treated as invalid with `inc = 0` and `carry = 0`. A `case` on `bcd` with a grouped arm for 0 through 8, an arm for 9 and a `default` for the invalid range expresses all of it in `always_comb`.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_bcd_increment(
    input  logic [3:0] bcd,
    output logic [3:0] inc,
    output logic       carry
);
```

#### Requirements
- Digits 0 through 8 increment normally with `carry = 0`.
- Digit 9 wraps: `inc = 0` and `carry = 1`.
- Values 10 to 15 are invalid: `inc = 0` and `carry = 0`, handled by the `default` arm.
- One `case (bcd)` inside `always_comb` produces both outputs.

#### Notes
The default arm here is not decoration: for a 4-bit input it really can fire, unlike the full-case decoders earlier in the track. Grouping the eight well-behaved digits into one arm with a comma list keeps the table short, and the whole module is the kind of helper a Verilog designer would write with nested ternaries and regret later.
solution_hints: Three behaviours, three case outcomes: increment, wrap, and refuse.
A comma-separated label list such as 4'd0, 4'd1 up to 4'd8 shares one arm.
The invalid rows never set carry; silence is not the same as a wrap.

title: Checker: Three-Sample Ordering Watchdog
description:
### Problem statement
Pipeline stages, sorters and sampling filters all assume their data arrives in order, and a watchdog proves it cheaply: `sorted` is 1 exactly when `x <= y` and `y <= z`, while the two `bad` flags name which neighbouring pair broke the order. All three outputs come from one `always_comb` block of relational comparisons.

#### Module interface
```systemverilog
module sv_check_sorted3(
    input  logic [3:0] x,
    input  logic [3:0] y,
    input  logic [3:0] z,
    output logic       sorted,
    output logic       bad_xy,
    output logic       bad_yz
);
```

#### Requirements
- `sorted` is 1 exactly for `x <= y` and `y <= z`.
- `bad_xy` is 1 exactly when `x` is greater than `y`; `bad_yz` is 1 exactly when `y` is greater than `z`.
- `sorted` and the bad flags must agree: sorted is 0 exactly when at least one bad flag is 1.
- Equal neighbours are in order.

#### Notes
The relational chain reads left to right like the specification, which is the quiet advantage of writing the checker in `always_comb` with `logic` ports: the block is three comparisons and an AND, with no `reg` bookkeeping and no sensitivity list to keep honest. Equal values are the boundary case the test plan leans on.
solution_hints: Two comparisons make the bad flags, and the sorted flag is the AND of their complements.
Equal neighbours are legal in every row that contains them, including 5 5 5.
Rows 5 and 7 break the order in the first pair only; one bad flag fires and the other stays low.
